planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring into moist, humus-rich, non-chalky soil in light to moderate shade; give it a sheltered site and winter mulch outside zone 8.

directions: Native to shaded forest margins in Taiwan, China, and Japan, this compact lacecap species prefers light to moderate shade, since full sun scorches its narrow, willow-like leaves. It flowers earlier than most hydrangeas, often in late spring, with airy white lacecap heads on a tidy mound well suited to a woodland edge or shaded border. It is less reliably cold-hardy than many garden hydrangeas, so give it protection outside its comfortable zone range.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring into fertile, well-drained soil in a wind-sheltered, partly shaded site.

directions: One of the hardiest Asian species hydrangeas, native to forested stream banks and mountain slopes across northern and central China, where it tolerates sun or fairly deep shade. Its chestnut-brown bark peels attractively with age, and flat white lacecap heads with reddish-aging sterile florets appear in summer on a substantial, upright shrub. It is markedly more cold-tolerant than most other Asian hydrangea species, reaching USDA zone 4.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring into reliably moist, humus-rich soil in light to dappled shade under high canopy.

directions: A central-Chinese forest species distinguished by huge, long-petioled, densely hairy leaves and wide lacecap flower heads up to 8 inches across. It is a true woodland-floor plant, performing best in light to dappled shade with reliably moist soil and sulking in hot sun. Use it as an architectural shade shrub beneath high canopy, where its oversized foliage and long leaf stalks read as a distinct textural accent.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring into moist but well-drained soil in partial to full shade; protect from hard freezes, since it is only reliably hardy from about zone 7 southward.

directions: A small, many-branched Japanese woodland shrub that genuinely prefers partial to full shade, unlike most garden hydrangeas, making it valuable for deeply shaded beds where sun-loving relatives struggle. It flowers early, in May and June, with small lacecap heads on slender branchlets and toothed, acuminate leaves, staying compact enough for a shaded foundation planting or understory grouping.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring into moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, sheltered from freezing winds.

directions: Native to woodland edges and scrub in Taiwan and the Philippines, this upright deutzia tolerates light shade better than most species in the genus, though full sun gives the heaviest bloom of drooping, lily-of-the-valley-like white-to-pink racemes. As stems mature they develop cinnamon-colored peeling bark reminiscent of a birch, giving winter interest beyond its spring flowers. It is less cold-hardy than the common garden deutzias, so site it with winter protection in marginal zones.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring into well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; prune immediately after flowering, since blooms form on the previous year's wood.

directions: A Japanese species notably more shade-tolerant than the already-present Deutzia gracilis or D. scabra, performing well in full sun to light afternoon shade, which makes it useful in hot-summer gardens where afternoon sun burns other deutzias. It bears clusters of small white star-shaped flowers along arching branches in late spring and is a low-maintenance, drought-tolerant shrub once established, good for borders, hedgerows, or woodland-edge plantings.
